You refuse to leave the doorway until you hear his footsteps.
You go looking for someone who has to give you an answer.
You tidy up, heat water, and prepare whatever might help if he returns hurt.
event.family_marine_07_no_return.title: He Doesn't Come Home
event.family_marine_07_no_return.text: Your father's patrol was due back before nightfall. Two hours after the bell, his spare coat still hangs untouched and nobody comes to explain the delay.
event.family_marine_07_no_return_i01_rum: Your imagination immediately fills in everything the neighbor does not know.
You force the neighbor to admit he is repeating something heard at the port.
You refuse to let the household panic over a story with no names and no proof.
A neighbor says one patrol boat was damaged. He does not know which one or who was aboard.
event.family_marine_07_no_return_i02_at_: The guard sends you home and tells your father you tried to push past him verbally.
The guard repeats the rule without adding a word.
He at least confirms your father is alive and the patrol is returning on foot.
He gives you an estimated return time and confirms your father is escorting an injured Marine.
You sit outside the restricted area and turn waiting into a silent protest.
You leave without a full answer, but with something concrete to do.
At the base, the guard has no orders to give you information. Behind him, empty stretchers have still been prepared.
event.family_marine_07_no_return_i03_ret: You do not blame the mission; you blame him for leaving you without knowing.
You put your fear aside until the injured Marine is settled and your father can finally speak.
You refuse reassuring phrases and make him recount the facts in order.
Your father finally returns, covered in salt and mud, another Marine's arm over his shoulders. He is not injured, but he immediately sees what his delay did to you.
event.family_marine_07_sealed_packet.cho: You put both hands on it and ask who sent it.
You damage the edge of the seal by handling it too closely.
You recognize nothing useful on the seal.
You recognize the same symbol used in the storehouse ledger.
You also notice the Marine who came for it belongs to a different service.
You hand the packet to the uniformed adult without asking anything.
event.family_marine_07_sealed_packet.tex: A petty officer leaves a sealed packet on the counter and asks you to guard it for five minutes while he fetches your father. Another Marine coat arrives almost immediately to collect it.
event.family_marine_07_sealed_packet_i01: You keep the packet out of reach until he proves something.
You ask for the same kind of proof adults demand from one another.
You finally hand it over because the uniform feels like enough proof.
The Marine asking for the packet does not know the name of the petty officer who gave it to you. He grows impatient when you ask.
event.family_marine_07_sealed_packet_i02: You muddle the details and sound as if you invented your reasons afterward.
You explain poorly, but the petty officer understands you hesitated for a reason.
You clearly reconstruct who asked for what and in what order.
You even identify the service difference that first made you suspicious.
You admit you treated the uniform itself as proof.
You maintain that guarding the packet was your job until proven otherwise.
The petty officer comes running back and stops when he sees the packet — or its absence — between you.
event.family_marine_07_sealed_packet_i03: You remember that an order does not erase the need to verify who it belongs to.
You mainly remember that adults will eventually correct their own mistakes.
You turn the hesitation or wrong handoff into a personal rule for next time.
The packet finally reaches the right hands. The petty officer lets you see the receipt before leaving, as if he wants you to know how trust is verified.
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name.choi: You let the praise land on you as if it already belonged to you.
Say you have done nothing yet
You point out that the name has not passed the exercise for you.
You promise so much that the other children burst out laughing.
Your confidence sounds borrowed rather than convincing.
You turn the praise into a challenge to the group.
Even the officer laughs and asks you to prove that confidence during the exercise.
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name.text: An officer praises you in front of other children before the exercise even starts: “With your father's name, we already know what to expect.”
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name_i01_: You refuse to defend merit you have not earned yet.
You suggest the exercise decide what the name cannot prove.
You openly accept that your family's history already gives you something.
Another child says loudly enough to be heard: “They're praising his father. He hasn't done anything.”
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name_i02_: You miss the simplest move exactly when everyone is watching.
You finish without distinction and without disaster.
You do well enough that the others finally talk about what you did.
You perform clearly well, and your father's name stops being the only thing the officer talks about.
You do only what is required, refusing to turn the drill into a performance.
Help the child who challenged you
You choose to help them with their drill instead of defending your name.
The drill starts with every eye on you. Every move now seems expected to confirm or deny a story that existed before you.
event.family_marine_07_fathers_name_i03_: You clearly separate what your father did from what you just did.
Say you will carry the name
You accept the name as an expectation, but decide to turn it into a responsibility.
You refuse to let your father's past become a verdict on your future.
After the drill, the officer starts talking about your father again. This time, you have something of your own to place beside that name.
You stay on the uniformed side while the vendor empties the stall.
Help the vendor save their goods
You start moving what can still be saved before anyone stops you.
Your question lands like an accusation and your father cuts you off in front of everyone.
You are only told that rules are rules.
Your father admits the punishment is broader than the offense.
You force the responsible officer to explain publicly why no middle option exists.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order.title: The Bad Order
event.family_marine_07_bad_order.text: A patrol shuts down a local vendor's stall for a minor violation. Your father enforces the order while the vendor protests that all the goods will spoil by tomorrow.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order_i01_rul: Read the notice with your father
You verify he did not invent the rule: it really exists.
You separate what can be carried away from what will be lost.
You look for a way to enforce the order without destroying everything on the stall.
The order is valid, signed, and simple. The problem is what it concretely does to the vendor when enforced without flexibility.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order_i02_per: Say that is the price of the rule
You accept that enforcing the rule carries that cost.
You do whatever the order does not explicitly forbid to reduce the damage.
Ask your father if it is fair
You refuse to ask only whether it is legal.
The vendor places a damaged crate at your feet: even if the order is lifted tomorrow, this part will not come back.
event.family_marine_07_bad_order_i03_fat: You decide the consistency of the rule matters more than what it cost today.
You keep the distinction between obeying correctly and doing something just.
Ask what he would do without the uniform
You force him to separate his personal judgment from the role he just carried out.
When the stall is empty, your father no longer has the rule in front of him. He now has to answer as your father, not only as a Marine.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list.choic: The organizer bristles and says he cannot rewrite the list for one person.
He promises to think about it next time, which solves nothing today.
He agrees to make a temporary place for you today.
He changes the list in front of you and asks what equipment is actually needed.
You suggest a version your body can actually take part in.
You refuse to stand around waiting for a box to appear for you.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list.title: Not on the List
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list.text: At an activity reserved for Marine families, the organizer looks for your name and stops: the column for your equipment or body type is blank.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list_i01_p: You refuse to let the decision be made away from you.
You take the equipment and show exactly what needs to change.
You leave before the adults turn your absence into a minor logistical detail.
The other families wait while the organizer decides: include you, improvise something, or continue without you.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list_i02_o: Invite them to try your version
A few try your adaptation and discover it works for them too.
Ask only for your own place
You refuse to prove the solution benefits everyone just to deserve a place.
The activity resumes, but your absence becomes visible instead of disappearing into an empty box.
The other children realize the decision made about you may change the activity for them too.
event.family_marine_07_not_on_list_i03_r: Make sure he changes the list
Your name and a concrete solution remain on the sheet after you leave.
You leave mainly knowing you can make your own place without waiting for perfect permission.
You do not forget how easily the organization continued without you.
At the end, the organizer keeps the sheet. He has to decide what he will write for next time.
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant.choi: The sergeant smiles as if he knows exactly which version you expect.
You ask him to leave out plaques, ranks, and polished words.
Say you do not want to hear it
The sergeant stops, but makes it clear he will keep the story if you change your mind.
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant.text: An old sergeant recognizes your name during a base formality. He says he served with your father and asks whether anyone ever told you “the broken bridge story.”
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant_i01_: You ask about the brave act before the mistake.
You focus on the mistake official stories could easily omit.
You refuse to choose which half of the story matters.
The sergeant says your father saved two comrades from a collapsed bridge — after ignoring an order that would have kept them away from it.
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant_i02_: Remember he went back for the others
You decide that making things right matters even when the mistake comes first.
You refuse to let the rescue erase the source of the danger.
You refuse to turn your father into either a pure hero or a pure fool.
The sergeant removes nothing: your father disobeyed out of pride, then risked his life to repair what his choice caused.
event.family_marine_07_old_sergeant_i03_: You choose to keep the courage without forgetting it came after a mistake.
You prefer a memory that resists polished stories.
Refuse to make it your story
You accept his past exists without deciding it must become your model.
The sergeant lets you leave with the one version he promises not to simplify if you ever ask again.
event.family_marine_07_giant_demonstrati: Do the planned test
You accept the announced program, no more and no less.
Choose the safest exercise
You choose the task least likely to turn your strength into a spectacle.
Ask what the test proves
They answer that the demonstration does not need your opinion to be useful.
The officer vaguely says they need numbers.
He admits they are already comparing your progress to other military profiles.
He explains exactly which performances would trigger closer monitoring.
The Demonstration
The officers have prepared weights, ropes, and targets to “see where you are.” This time, they ask in front of several adults what you are actually willing to demonstrate.
Lift cleanly
The load tips and slips from your grip.
You move forward, but the load drifts toward the edge of the lane.
You control the load and still have room to spare.
You finish with enough control that the officers stop talking only about raw strength.
Take more time
You refuse to turn the test into a race and keep the load under control.
Ask for a spotter
You demand a safety measure nobody had planned for the visitors.
The Test Begins
The first task looks simple: move a load to a mark without leaving the lane painted on the ground.
Finish your move first
You finish the exercise before turning toward the accident.
Drop the test and protect the helper
You immediately abandon the performance to block the crate's path.
Shout for them to move
You use your voice before your strength to get the helper out of danger.
The Rope Gives
A restraint rope snaps behind you. A small equipment crate starts sliding toward a young helper standing too close to the area.
Defend your choice
You lose your temper and the officer reduces the discussion to your attitude.
He insists the test should have been completed even though nobody was hurt.
You make him admit that a Marine who ignores someone in danger has failed something more important than a timer.
Even the other officers repeat your argument before the supervisor can close the discussion.
Accept their scoring
You let the adults decide the measurable performance was the only important part.
Ask if the helper is okay first
You refuse to discuss the score before checking the person who was endangered.
What Actually Counts
The accident is over. The responsible officer looks first at the timer, then at the helper, then at you.
Make them record the protective choice
The note in your file mentions protection before performance.
Make them record the best result
You choose to make the file remember first what your body can do.
Make them record your safety conditions
You make them record that the next demonstration cannot be organized as if nobody else exists around it.
What They Write Down
The officers fill out the same kind of notebook as four years earlier. This time, you can see whether the line records only strength or judgment too.
event.family_marine_07_not_an_exhibit.ch: You leave before he finishes the introduction.
Say no in front of them
Your anger lets the officer present your refusal as a tantrum.
He smiles and tries to continue despite your refusal.
The visitors stop and wait for your answer rather than the officer's.
One visitor directly asks why you were brought there without your agreement.
You interrupt the officer and decide what will be shown.
event.family_marine_07_not_an_exhibit.te: Despite your earlier refusal, an officer is waiting with three visitors from another service. He presents your size and growth before even asking whether you want to stay.
event.family_marine_07_not_an_exhibit_i0: Speak to the visitors, not the officer
You explain directly to them what you are refusing.
Ask them to leave
You change the question: you are no longer the one expected to leave.
Accept one test you choose
You agree to show one thing only because you set the limit.
The Visitors Wait
The discomfort becomes obvious: the visitors realize they are watching something that was never negotiated with you.
Let him save face
You get to leave, but he still gets to explain why.
Correct his version in front of them
You refuse to let your consent be invented after the fact.
Ask where your father is in this decision
You bring the scene back to the family the officer claims to represent.
Saving Face
The officer tries to reframe the scene as a misunderstanding. He wants everyone to leave believing the Marine had planned for your refusal.
State what cannot happen again
You turn your refusal into an explicit rule for any future summons.
Decide not to cooperate again
You now refuse any tracking that begins without your agreement.
Only agree when you present yourself
You keep the door open only if nobody speaks about you before you do.
Your Boundary
The visitors finally leave. What remains matters more for the future: the officer now knows exactly what boundary you set and whether he respected it.
event.family_marine_07_what_marines_prot: Wait for the equipment
You stay behind the line while the trapped civilians beg everyone to hurry.
Help before the order
You get too close and part of the cart shifts dangerously.
You cannot free anyone alone and the watch commander orders you back.
You clear enough space for one civilian to breathe more easily.
You find a leverage point that lets the adults begin before all the equipment arrives.
Bring the Marines to the civilians
You pull Marines toward the trapped civilians one by one instead of waiting for the order to change.
What the Marine Protects
An overturned cart blocks a street near a Marine post. Two civilians are trapped beneath it, but the watch commander orders everyone to wait for proper equipment before moving anything.
Stay behind the line
You accept that group safety comes before the visible urgency beneath the cart.
Find a safe support
You look for a way to reduce the risk without completely ignoring the order.
Ask your father what he would do
You ask him while both the order and the trapped people are still in front of him.
It Gets Worse
A wheel cracks under the weight. By the time the equipment arrives, the cart may shift again.
Convince him to start
He sends you firmly behind the line and bans further improvisation.
He still refuses, but orders the equipment rushed in.
He authorizes a limited move using what is already secured.
He adopts your idea, assigns roles, and begins the rescue immediately.
Accept the wait
You stop pushing against the order and help prepare for the equipment.
Disobey to protect
You choose the trapped person over the exact form of the order.
Act Under Pressure
The watch commander now has to choose between maintaining the order exactly or using what you have already prepared.
Defend the procedure
You remember that protecting people also means avoiding new victims.
Defend acting quickly
You remember that an order preventing protection may need to be challenged.
Defend the safer third way
You mainly remember that obeying and disobeying were not the only two options.
After the Rescue
The civilians are finally freed. The argument continues after the emergency: did you act correctly because everyone is safe, or despite the way you acted?
event.family_marine_07_fallback_home_dut: You start by protecting the house.
You start with what will be hardest to replace.
You start with what is directly waiting for your father.
Your father leaves three things to do before he returns: close the shutters, fetch water, and keep the meal warm. Only one can be done immediately.
You show him you did not forget the other tasks, only chose which one could least afford to wait.
You simply finish the list instead of seeking his approval.
Give one task back to him
You remind him that holding the household together has not become only your job.
Your father returns earlier than expected and immediately sees the order in which you chose to hold the household together.
event.family_marine_07_fallback_service_: Follow the protocol exactly
You repeat the gestures you were shown.
Ask what it is for
You interrupt the ritual before reproducing it.
Add a personal note
You slip something personal into a service formality.
Service as Inheritance
Each year your household must hand a small service record or insignia to the local office. This time, the adult asks you to make the handoff yourself.
Accept the ritual
You understand the gesture exists precisely because it repeats.
Say what it means to you
You refuse to let the office decide alone what the gesture means.
Make the handoff and nothing more
You complete the formality without giving it more weight.
Why We Do It
The clerk explains that the handoff serves both the archives and as a reminder of which families remain tied to service.
Keep it as a Marine tradition
You accept that the institution is part of how your family tells its story.
Keep it as a family tradition
You reclaim the ritual for the household rather than the office.
Treat it as routine
You learn to move through the institution without giving meaning to every gesture.
The Gesture That Remains
The clerk files the document. The ritual is over, but you chose whether it belonged mostly to the Marine, your family, or simply the calendar.
event.family_marine_07_fallback_belongin: Say exactly what you need
You give a solution before anyone offers a bad one.
Try their first idea
You agree to test their first idea before judging it.
Adapt on your own
You begin moving the equipment without waiting.
Finding Your Place
A base activity once again needs adjusting for your body. This time, the adults look directly at you instead of trying to guess what you need.
Fix it with them
You explain the new problem before it becomes a new habit.
Make do
You accept an imperfect solution so the activity can continue.
Start over differently
You refuse to let a half-working adaptation become the standard.
An Imperfect Solution
The first adaptation works halfway. It solves one problem and creates another.
Remember it can be fixed together
You keep the idea that an institution can learn if someone clearly says what does not work.
Remember you can make do
You learn to move forward even when the system only adapts halfway.
Keep your own method
You trust what you build yourself more than solutions designed for you.
Your Way of Doing It
When the activity finally begins, nobody can pretend the solution appeared on its own.
